messages.author: 9d7e54e3329f305f
messages.subject: GMRF / CAR model - initialization/acceptance problems
parts:
Hello all,

I'm attempting to fit a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model in Stan. To begin with, I'm just trying to replicate the Scotland Lip Cancer example from GeoBUGS.

I've opted to use a more generalized GMRF with a CAR covariance in order to allow for joint sampling in Stan. Equation 3 of this paper gives one such formulation, which is what I've tried to implement. (This paper gives another, slightly different formulation.)

The model (attached or below) compiles but fails to initialize ("Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."). I've tried a wide range of priors/initial values with no success.

In Knorr-Held & Rue 2001 they implement a "Cholesky factor algorithm" in order to draw from GMRFs with a much higher acceptance rate. However, this would require subsampling (running their algorithm for the GMRF proposal inside every step in the overall model fitting).

Can anyone suggest ways to fit the model? I'm guessing the subsampling algorithm might be the ultimate direction I'll have to go down, but not quite sure how to implement it in Stan.

Thanks for any suggestions!
Kyle

ps I haven't yet tried optimizing the model for speed aside from vectorization, but I'm sure there is plenty of room for improvement in that respect.

data {
    int<lower=1> N;     // number of areas
    vector[N] O;        // observed cases
    vector[N] E;        // expected cases
    vector[N] x;        // covariate (pct agric)
    matrix[N,N] A;      // area adjacency matrix
}
transformed data {
    matrix[N,N] D;      // diagonal matrix with d_ii = sum(c_ij)
    for (i in 1:N)
        for (j in 1:N)
            D[i,j] <- if_else(i==j, sum(row(A, i)), 0.0);
}
parameters {
    real alpha0;            // intercept
    real alpha1;            // coefficient on covariate
    vector[N] beta1;        // area-specific random effect (CAR)
    real<lower=0> tau;      // precision of CAR
    real<lower=0,upper=1> p;// strength of spatial correlation
}
transformed parameters {
    real sigma_sq;
    vector[N] zeros;        // zeros for mean of MVN
    sigma_sq <- 1 / (tau * tau);
    for (i in 1:N)
        zeros[i] <- 0.0;    
                // not sure if transformed parameters is the best place for this
}
model {
    // declarations
        matrix[N,N] Sigma;  // covariance matrix for CAR
        real beta1_mean;
        vector[N] beta1_stz;
        vector[N] log_mu;
        vector[N] mu;
    // priors on model parameters
        // no prior on alpha0 (improper flat prior)
        alpha1 ~ normal(0.0, 100.0);
        tau ~ gamma(0.5, 0.0005);
    // covariance matrix
        Sigma <- sigma_sq * inverse(D - p * A);
            // note: look into efficiencies of matrix inversion in stan
            // may also set p=1 and move inverse(D-A) into transformed parameters
    // CAR model
        beta1 ~ multi_normal(zeros, Sigma);
            // more efficient parameterizations in stan?
    // impose sum-to-zero constraint on CAR
        beta1_mean <- mean(beta1);
        beta1_stz <- beta1 - beta1_mean;
    // model prediction
        log_mu <- log(E) + alpha0 + alpha1 * x + beta1_stz;
        mu <- exp(log_mu);
    // likelihood
        O ~ poisson(mu);
}

Right. I guess you figured this out but for anyone else who may later Google this thread, whereas GeoBUGS has these conditional auto-regressive priors where the distribution of one element of a vector is known given all the other elements of the vector, in Stan you need to be using whatever joint distribution is implied by the union of these conditionals distributions.

The model (attached or below) compiles but fails to initialize ("Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."). I've tried a wide range of priors/initial values with no success.

And there are much faster ways to deal with the covariance matrix that we can help you with once we get to that point.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: GMRF / CAR model - initialization/acceptance problems
parts: On Friday, February 1, 2013 11:19:39 AM UTC-5, Kyle Foreman wrote:
Can anyone suggest ways to fit the model? I'm guessing the subsampling algorithm might be the ultimate direction I'll have to go down, but not quite sure how to implement it in Stan.

It turns out that the fundamental cause of the problem is that it has numerical problems with inverse(), and that causes the gradient to have nans, and that causes some proposed parameters to be nan. Replace all this

// covariance matrix
        Sigma <- sigma_sq * inverse(D - p * A);
            // note: look into efficiencies of matrix inversion in stan
            // may also set p=1 and move inverse(D-A) into transformed parameters
    // CAR model
        beta1 ~ multi_normal(zeros, Sigma);
            // more efficient parameterizations in stan?

with

lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 / sigma_sq * (beta1' * D * beta1 - p * (beta1' * A * beta1)); // MVN prior on beta1

Also, it would be better to change all this

// model prediction
        log_mu <- log(E) + alpha0 + alpha1 * x + beta1_stz;
        mu <- exp(log_mu);
    // likelihood
        O ~ poisson(mu);

to

log_mu <- log(E) + alpha0 + alpha1 * x + beta1_stz;
O ~ poisson_log(log_mu);

Ben

Crap. I forgot to include the determinant part of the multivariate normal. I should have said to also add this line:

Apologies for the radio silence, I got sidetracked with paper writing and just came back to this project yesterday.

Using Ben's lp method for explicitly writing out the MVN without requiring inversion (attached, model1.txt - and thanks again, Ben!), it runs quickly and comes up with mean estimates similar to those of bugs for alpha0 and sigma:
  • sigma
    • bugs
      • mean:  .65
      • sd:  .11
    • stan
      • mean:  .7
      • sd  .1
  • alpha0
    • bugs
      • mean:  -.30
      • sd:  .11
    • stan
      • mean:  -.2
      • sd:  .1
At first glance the betas are reasonable, but I'm having trouble getting OpenBUGS to run on OSX right now so I haven't yet directly compared for specific regions.

The main difference thus far is alpha1 (which is the coefficient on the covariate):

  • alpha1
    • bugs
      • mean:  .46
      • sd:  .12
    • stan
      • mean:  .0
      • sd:  .0
Not sure why alpha0 stays at zero. I'm using a relatively weak prior [N(0,1e5) to match with bugs' N(0,1e-5)] and have experimented with lots of different values for the precision. I've also tried changing the initial value from 0, but it always ends up back there, even with extreme initials.

Sorry there's not more to report on that front, but I'll continue experimenting and see if I can't get figure out what's going on there. Any ideas are again appreciated!

I've also tried using the new multi_normal_prec. The thought was I could avoid the computationally expensive inversions but still use the probability distribution convenience functions instead of relying on lp -=.

The version using multi_normal_prec is attached as model2.txt. It picks absolutely gigantic values for tau (on the order of 1e6, compared to ~1.3 for model1), which translates to a sigma close to 0. There's not much documentation in the source for multi_normal_prec yet, so maybe I'm missing something there. I've simply used MVN_prec(0 vector, (D - p * A) * tau^2). 

John, I can't yet give you a good speed comparison, but once I have the model working well I'll look into it and post to the list.

On Sunday, February 24, 2013 5:50:58 PM UTC-5, Kyle Foreman wrote:
Not sure why alpha0 stays at zero. I'm using a relatively weak prior [N(0,1e5) to match with bugs' N(0,1e-5)] and have experimented with lots of different values for the precision. I've also tried changing the initial value from 0, but it always ends up back there, even with extreme initials.
That doesn't quite match up. In Stan, 1e5 is a standard deviation, while in the BUGS-family 1e-5 is a precision. With sqrt(1e5), I get alpha0 to move a little bit away from zero.

I've also tried using the new multi_normal_prec. The thought was I could avoid the computationally expensive inversions but still use the probability distribution convenience functions instead of relying on lp -=.

The version using multi_normal_prec is attached as model2.txt. It picks absolutely gigantic values for tau (on the order of 1e6, compared to ~1.3 for model1), which translates to a sigma close to 0. There's not much documentation in the source for multi_normal_prec yet, so maybe I'm missing something there. I've simply used MVN_prec(0 vector, (D - p * A) * tau^2).

That's the right syntax, I think.

Ben
